questions.topic: the pipeline as the only way
questions.scenario: Engineers can still change production settings in the portal during incidents, and the next pipeline run keeps undoing their fixes.
options: Run the pipeline less often
Make the pipeline the only way to production: configuration in code, engineers on Reader with PIM for emergencies, and emergency fixes committed back to code
Stop using infrastructure as code
Let the portal win whenever there is a conflict
questions.explanation: Two ways into production guarantee drift. Keeping configuration in code and access read-only, with a controlled emergency path whose changes flow back into code, makes the pipeline the single source of truth.

questions.scenario: A new product team's code is on GitHub. An older team runs a reliable Azure Pipeline to an on-premises server and tracks business work in Azure Boards.
questions.stem: What is the most pragmatic approach?
options: Force both teams onto one tool immediately
Use GitHub and Actions for the new product, keep the working Azure Pipeline and Boards, and give each tool a clear job
Duplicate every repository in both tools
Move everything to a third tool
questions.explanation: Start where the code and the team already are, and migrate only when running both costs more than moving. Both toolchains deploy to Azure well, and they integrate. Duplication creates two sources of truth.

questions.scenario: A continuously deployed API uses long-lived feature branches merged every few weeks, with painful conflicts and big-bang releases.
options: GitFlow with more release branches
Trunk-based development: short-lived branches, small pull requests, main always releasable, and feature flags for unfinished work
Committing straight to main without review
One branch per environment
questions.explanation: Frequent, small integration keeps conflicts small and main deployable, and flags let unfinished work merge safely. Branch-per-environment models make environments diverge, and skipping review removes the quality gate.

questions.scenario: An administrator bypassed branch protection to push a hotfix, which broke the build for a day.
questions.stem: What should the protection rules include?
options: An exemption for administrators
Rules that apply to administrators too, with required checks and approvals, and any emergency bypass logged and reviewed
Fewer required checks
Protection only on release branches
questions.explanation: Controls the most privileged people can skip fail when pressure is highest. Applying them to everyone, with an auditable emergency path, keeps main protected.

questions.scenario: A fix passed in test but failed in production because the pipeline rebuilt the code for each environment.
options: Rebuild with pinned tool versions
Build once, publish the artefact, and deploy that same artefact to every environment
Skip test to avoid the difference
Build in production only
questions.explanation: Promoting a single artefact guarantees production runs exactly what was tested. Separate builds can still differ in subtle ways, and skipping test removes the check.

questions.scenario: A GitHub Actions workflow deploys with a client secret stored in repository secrets, and any branch can use it.
options: Rotate the secret monthly
OIDC federation with a separate Azure identity per GitHub environment, scoped to its resource group, and deployment branch rules on production
Store the secret in a variable file in the repository
Use one identity with Owner on the subscription for all environments
questions.explanation: Federation removes the stored secret, binding identities to environments keeps production credentials out of other jobs, and branch rules stop feature branches reaching production. Rotation and broader scope keep or worsen the risk.

questions.scenario: An Azure Pipelines production approval is implemented as a manual step in the YAML file, and a developer removes it in a pull request.
options: In a comment at the top of the YAML
On the production environment's approvals and checks, which the YAML cannot remove
In the pipeline's README
Nowhere; approvals slow delivery
questions.explanation: Environment checks are enforced by the platform whenever a deployment targets the environment, so editing the pipeline file cannot bypass them. Controls in the file can be removed in the same change that needs them removed.

questions.scenario: A Bicep pull request renames the production SQL database to match a new naming convention.
questions.stem: What should stop the data loss?
options: Nothing; Azure renames resources in place
The what-if output on the pull request showing a Delete for the old database, read by reviewers before approving
A faster pipeline
A larger database tier
questions.explanation: Renaming a resource in code means deleting it and creating a new one. What-if or plan output on every infrastructure pull request exposes destructive changes, and reviewers must read the Delete lines.

questions.scenario: Production no longer matches the Bicep in main after several portal changes during incidents.
options: Export the current state over the code
Prevent it with read-only access and policy, detect it with a scheduled what-if, and resolve each difference by updating code or re-applying it
Ignore it until the next deployment
Stop using infrastructure as code
questions.explanation: Prevention, detection and deliberate resolution keep code and reality in agreement. Exporting state over code makes unreviewed changes permanent, and ignoring drift lets the next deployment undo fixes unpredictably.

questions.scenario: A production API key was committed three weeks ago; a developer removed it in a later commit.
options: Nothing; it is gone
Rotate the key immediately, then clean history and store the new key in Key Vault, with push protection to prevent a repeat
Make the repository private
Rename the variable
questions.explanation: The key lives on in history, clones and forks, so it must be assumed compromised and replaced first. Push protection stops recognised secrets reaching the repository in future.

questions.scenario: A workflow uses third-party actions by tag, the build job holds production deploy credentials, and production pulls images tagged latest.
questions.stem: Which changes reduce supply-chain risk most?
options: Use @master for actions to get fixes faster
Pin actions to commit SHAs, keep production credentials only in the deploy job, and deploy images by digest with verified provenance
Run the workflow less often
Make the registry public
questions.explanation: Pinned actions cannot be silently swapped, separating untrusted build code from credentials limits what a compromised dependency can reach, and digest-plus-provenance ensures production runs only what the pipeline built.

questions.scenario: A checkout release to everyone at once failed 8% of payments, and rolling back by rebuilding took 40 minutes.
questions.stem: What release approach fits the API on App Service?
options: Release less often
Deploy to a staging slot, smoke test, route a small canary share gated on SLO comparisons, then swap - keeping swap-back as a seconds-long rollback
Deploy directly to production at night
Rebuild faster
questions.explanation: Slots and canaries separate deploying from releasing: few users see the new version first, metrics decide whether it proceeds, and swapping back restores the previous version instantly.

questions.scenario: After a swap back, the previous version fails because the new release had renamed a database column.
options: Never roll back
Expand and contract: add new structures first, migrate, and remove old ones in a later release, so each schema change works with the previous code
Keep the database in a deployment slot
Only change the database on weekends
questions.explanation: Code rolls back in seconds; data does not. Keeping every schema change compatible with the previous version means rollbacks always meet a database they understand.

questions.scenario: The CTO asks whether delivery is improving. The team reports story points completed per sprint.
options: Lines of code per developer
The DORA metrics - deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore - as trends for the team, alongside SLOs
Number of pipeline runs
Hours worked
questions.explanation: The DORA metrics measure delivery outcomes, pairing speed with stability, and SLOs show the user's experience. Effort and activity measures say little about outcomes and are easily gamed.
